DARVO.short_definition: A three-part reply to being confronted: deny it happened, attack the person raising it, then claim to be the one who was wronged.
DARVO.core_meaning: A three-part reply to being confronted: deny it happened, attack the person raising it, then claim to be the one who was wronged.
DARVO.expanded_definition: DARVO stands for Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender. Psychologist Jennifer Freyd named it in the late 1990s. Someone is told their behavior hurt another person. They say it did not happen, turn on the person who spoke up, and end up describing themselves as the one under attack. The listener then spends the talk defending themselves, and the first complaint is never answered. One defensive flash after a surprising accusation is common. The pattern shows when all three moves arrive together and come back each time.
DARVO.plain_language_summary: You bring up something that hurt you. Within minutes you are the one saying sorry, because they have become the injured one.
DARVO.why_this_matters: People who raise a hard subject often do it at real cost. When the reply turns them into the accused, they can leave convinced the original problem was never real, or that speaking up is not worth the price.
what_it_is: A sequence of three moves, not one: refusing the facts, going after the person who raised them, and then taking the role of the hurt party.
It often shows up after someone describes harm directly, such as in a confrontation, a complaint to a manager, or a public accusation.
The attack usually borrows from the complaint itself, so the words 'hurt', 'abuse' or 'lied' get handed back to the person who said them.
The reversal can be sincere on the speaker's side. Someone can feel truly wronged by being accused, and the pattern is still visible in the exchange.
what_it_sounds_like: That never happened, and I can't believe you'd say it.
Oh, so now I'm the villain?
After everything I've put up with from you, you have the nerve to accuse me?
You're the one who's been cruel to me.
I'm the real victim here, and you know it.
I'm getting hurt just listening to this.
You always twist things so you look innocent.
what_it_is_not: A person who is falsely accused and says, with specifics, which part is wrong. Disputing a claim is different from reversing the roles.
A two-sided conflict in which both people carry real grievances and each gets a turn to be heard.
Visible hurt or tears from someone told they caused harm. Feeling wounded is not the same as flipping the blame.
A first, defensive burst of denial that settles into 'let me think about what you said' after a few minutes or a day.
A counter-complaint that is raised after the first one has been answered, and is treated as a separate matter.
this_may_be_it_when: Within the same conversation, you go from raising a concern to defending your own character.
The other person describes you as the abusive, cruel or dishonest one, using the same words you used about them.
The original complaint is not mentioned again once the argument turns to your behavior.
The same reversal follows each time you raise something similar, whatever the topic.
You leave feeling you owe an apology for having spoken at all.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They answer your complaint point by point first, and only then raise something of their own.
Their counter-claim has real support, such as a message or a witness, and is open to the same checking as yours.
The denial concerns one fact they can show is wrong, with no attack on you attached.
Both of you are able to say 'I hurt you' and 'you hurt me' within the same talk.
They come back later and take up your original point without being asked.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Being accused of something hurtful is painful, and people often lash out in the first minute before they can think clearly.
The accusation may have been delivered in a harsh or public way that made self-protection feel urgent.
Some people were raised in homes where admitting fault brought punishment, so denial is a learned reflex and not a plan.
They may truly remember the event differently, and be as sure of their memory as you are of yours.
common_false_positives: A coworker falsely accused of a mistake who says 'that wasn't me, here is the log', and then asks why you thought it was.
A couple fighting where each person feels unheard, and both say 'you are the one hurting me'.
A friend who snaps back in the moment and sends an apology the next morning that deals with the actual issue.
discernment_questions: Did anyone answer what I first raised, even once, before the talk moved to my behavior?
Are the three moves (denial, attack, role reversal) all present, or is it only a short flash of defensiveness?
Does this reversal happen each time I bring up this kind of subject?
If someone else heard a recording of this conversation, would they say the complaint was ever addressed?
Is there anything in their counter-accusation that is checkable and true, which I should take seriously?
less_concerning_if: The reversal fades once things calm down, and the original subject is picked up again.
The counter-complaint is specific, supportable and discussed as a second matter.
They can say 'I felt attacked' without also saying 'so you are the problem'.
more_concerning_if: They tell other people you are the one who has been abusive, before or after you have spoken up.
They threaten to report you, take your children or involve your employer in response to your complaint.
You have started to rehearse apologies before you raise anything, or to drop subjects entirely.
pattern_over_time_signs: Complaints you once raised openly are now kept to yourself because they end in a fight about you.
You keep a list of your own past mistakes close at hand, ready for when the reversal comes.
Mutual friends or family have heard their account of events more than yours.
Months later you cannot say what your first complaint was, only that you ended up sorry.
DARVO.repair_check: Repair here would mean going back to the first complaint and answering it, including the part they dispute, before any counter-claim gets a turn. Warning signs are a general 'sorry things got heated' that never touches the original point, or an apology that arrives only after you have apologized.
DARVO.boundary_respect_check: Watch what happens to your original concern after you ask to finish it first. Does it get a reply, a date to continue, or a promise to return to it? Or does the conversation snap back to your character within a minute or two?
DARVO.psychological_mechanism: In an online vignette study, Harsey, Zurbriggen and Freyd (2017) linked exposure to DARVO-style replies with more self-blame. Being cast as the wrongdoer right after speaking up can pull attention onto clearing your own name, and the first complaint tends to slide out of view.
DARVO.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe leaving a confrontation feeling guilty and confused, sometimes apologizing for the very thing they came to raise. Some go quiet about later problems, because the last time cost too much. Others replay the conversation for days trying to find where it turned.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the order of events calmly: 'I came to talk about the missed payment, and now we are talking about me. Can we finish the first subject?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for the first matter to be written down so it is not lost: 'Could we put my original point on paper? I'll read your concern too.' Keep the request mild.
response_options.disengagement: When the talk turns to your character, ask whether the original point can be written down, then take a break without announcing a return time or a conclusion.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted person what you originally raised and what happened next. Hearing 'that is not what you came to talk about' from someone outside can restore your footing.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Put the original complaint in writing with dates before any meeting, and ask HR or a manager to keep the discussion on that record when a counter-complaint appears.

DARVO.boundary_script: "I can see you're upset, and I will listen to that. But I came here to talk about the missed dinner and the lie about it. Can we stay on that first, and then take your concerns right after?"
DARVO.safety_note: DARVO can show up alongside abuse, where a person who reports harm is then described to others as the one who caused the harm. Watch for threats to report you, to call your employer, or to claim custody, and for fear of what happens if you push back. Domestic violence advocates and legal aid can help you plan. If the counter-accusations are joined by threats of violence, call your local emergency number instead of waiting to see how it plays out.
misuse_warning: Anyone who is angry at being accused can sound like this for a minute. Naming DARVO after one defensive reply shuts down a conversation that might have recovered.
People who really have caused harm sometimes say 'that is DARVO' about any pushback they receive. The word does not settle who is right.
DARVO.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Blame-Shifting puts the cause of the act on you but does not necessarily claim to be injured. Whataboutism answers with a different past complaint and does not deny or attack. Denial only refuses the facts. DARVO ends by casting the accuser as the wrongdoer and the accused as the victim.

Blame-Shifting.short_definition: Placing the cause of your own action on the other person, so that your choice is described as something they did to you.
Blame-Shifting.core_meaning: Placing the cause of your own action on the other person, so that your choice is described as something they did to you.
Blame-Shifting.expanded_definition: Blame-shifting takes a real action, such as a shout, a missed promise or a broken thing, and moves its cause onto someone else. 'I did it' becomes 'you made me do it.' Context does matter in real conflicts, and naming it once is not the problem. The pattern appears when the other person's behavior is offered as a complete explanation, leaving no room for the speaker's own choice, and when this repeats across different events. The person who was harmed ends up holding both the injury and the fault.
Blame-Shifting.plain_language_summary: Someone does something hurtful, then explains it as your doing. By the end you are apologizing for causing what they chose to do.
Blame-Shifting.why_this_matters: If every hurtful act is explained as a reaction to you, you can end up policing your own behavior to head off theirs. That is a heavy job nobody can do, and it keeps the real problem from ever being talked about.
what_it_is: An explanation that treats the speaker's choice as if it were forced on them by what you said or did.
It usually follows a specific act: raised voices, a forgotten task, a broken agreement, or a mistake at work.
The cause sits in the past tense of your behavior, such as 'if you had called', and the speaker's own option to act differently is missing.
It tends to include a list of your faults offered as proof, whether or not those faults relate to what happened.
what_it_sounds_like: Look what you made me do.
I wouldn't have yelled if you had just answered the phone.
You drove me to it.
If you hadn't brought up money, none of this would have happened.
You know how I get when you do that, so this is on you.
I only lied because you would have overreacted.
You brought this on yourself.
what_it_is_not: Honestly describing a real trigger, such as 'I was exhausted and your comment landed badly', while still owning the response.
A mutual conflict where both people admit what they added and neither claims to be the only cause.
A true statement of fact about timing, such as 'I was late because the train was canceled'.
A child or very stressed adult who blames the nearest person in the heat of the moment, then settles and takes responsibility.
Explaining your reasons for a decision without claiming the other person left you no option.
this_may_be_it_when: Every time something goes wrong, the explanation leads back to something you did or did not do.
The phrase 'you made me' or 'you forced me' is used for actions that were clearly a choice.
You find yourself changing your behavior to prevent their reactions, such as speaking less, hiding purchases or avoiding certain subjects.
Their own part, even a small one, is never named, even after you raise it calmly.
An apology from you is expected before anything is discussed.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They name your part and theirs in the same breath, with something like 'I shouldn't have said that, though I was hurt'.
The explanation is limited to one real event and is not repeated across different ones.
They accept that you could not have predicted how they would respond.
You can point to something you did that really did contribute, and they do not inflate it.
Afterwards, they change what they do, not what you do.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People under heavy stress often grab for an outside cause first and find their own part only later.
Some families teach that anger is always caused by someone else, so the habit is inherited rather than chosen.
Your own behavior may truly have been unkind, and the explanation is partly accurate even if incomplete.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'I snapped because I was waiting on that message all day' and then apologizes for snapping.
A manager who points out that a deadline slipped because a handoff was late, while still taking responsibility for the plan.
Two siblings arguing about who started it, each partly right, with no one using it to avoid owning their own part.
discernment_questions: Did they do something that was within their own control to do differently?
Does the explanation leave any share at all for their own choice?
Has my behavior changed to avoid setting them off, and has that helped?
Does this explanation appear after most conflicts, or just this one?
If a friend of mine did the same thing and gave the same reason, would I accept it as a full account?
less_concerning_if: They add 'that was still my choice' to the sentence, even grudgingly.
They are able to describe their own part once things have cooled.
The reason they offer is a fact about the situation and not about your character.
more_concerning_if: The blame is attached to anger, shoving, damaged belongings or threats, and it is used to explain these.
You have started to apologize for their outbursts as if you had caused them.
Other people around you have begun repeating that you are the cause of their moods.
pattern_over_time_signs: You keep a mental checklist of things not to say, and the list grows rather than shrinks.
Their outbursts persist even after you have changed what they said set them off.
You notice you are apologizing for events that happened before you arrived.
Friends comment that you seem to walk on eggshells around them.
Blame-Shifting.repair_check: Repair would sound like 'that was my decision' with no 'but' attached, and it would show the next time the same trigger appears: the shout, the lie or the slammed door does not happen, and you are not asked to prevent it. A list of what you did to cause it is the opposite.
Blame-Shifting.boundary_respect_check: After you say the reaction was theirs to choose, notice whether they pause and engage with that, or whether a new charge arrives, such as being cold, unfair or unwilling to take any responsibility yourself. The blame may have only moved to a new place.
Blame-Shifting.psychological_mechanism: Many people accept responsibility quickly, especially for someone they care about or after being told they are difficult. Repeated, confident blame can draw on that readiness, so the receiver starts auditing their own conduct before the event itself, and the other person's choice drops out of the picture.
Blame-Shifting.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe constantly monitoring what they say, apologizing for outbursts they did not cause, and losing track of where their own responsibility starts and ends. Some grow quieter or more anxious around the person, and some begin hiding things to avoid setting off a reaction.

response_options.soft_clarification: Keep the question narrow and calm: 'I can see I upset you. Can we go through what happened, step by step?' Leave the trigger-versus-choice question for a counselor or mediator.
response_options.firm_boundary: Say once what you will take responsibility for: 'I'll talk about what I said.' Ask to go through the rest in order, with a neutral person present if you can.
response_options.disengagement: When the explanation turns to your faults, ask for a short pause, such as a drink of water, and let the topic wait without announcing a verdict or a return time.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe a specific incident to someone outside the relationship and ask whether the cause they hear sounds like yours. Outsiders often notice the shift in blame before you do.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Record what happened in neutral terms, with dates and who did what, and ask for the discussion to cover each person's actions separately, not who caused whom.

Blame-Shifting.boundary_script: "I can see that I upset you, and I'm willing to talk about my part. I'd also like us to go through what happened next, step by step. Could someone else sit in?"
Blame-Shifting.safety_note: Blame-shifting in an ordinary argument is a communication problem. Concern rises when you are blamed for someone's shouting, breaking things or physical force, or told you deserve it, because you may then be made responsible for managing their anger. Fear of their reaction or any injury is the signal. A domestic abuse advocate or trusted person can help you plan. If you are hurt or afraid for your life, call the emergency number where you live.
misuse_warning: People are sometimes accused of blame-shifting for mentioning any context at all. Explaining what led up to something is fair. The concern is explanations that leave no room for the speaker's own choice.
Using the label to avoid hearing a legitimate point about your own contribution turns it into a way of dodging.
Blame-Shifting.how_to_distinguish_from_related: DARVO adds a denial and an attack, then makes the speaker the victim. Blame-Shifting can come with a calm admission of the act, so long as its cause is placed on you. Whataboutism points to a separate wrong of yours instead. Denial refuses that the act happened at all.

Whataboutism.short_definition: Answering a complaint by raising a different wrong from the other side, so that the original issue goes unanswered.
Whataboutism.core_meaning: Answering a complaint by raising a different wrong from the other side, so that the original issue goes unanswered.
Whataboutism.expanded_definition: Whataboutism meets a complaint with a counter-complaint about something else, usually older or from a different topic. 'What about the time you forgot my birthday?' The tit-for-tat can feel fair, because both things may be real. The problem is the swap. The first concern is set aside as if the two cancel out, and the talk ends in a draw with nothing resolved. Raising your own grievance is reasonable. It becomes this pattern when it replaces the answer instead of following it.
Whataboutism.plain_language_summary: You raise a problem, and instead of a reply you get a different problem about you. Both end up unsolved, and the talk feels like a tie.
Whataboutism.why_this_matters: When each complaint is met with another one, nothing is ever finished. Real issues pile up unresolved, and the person who raised the first one starts to wonder if it was fair to speak at all.
what_it_is: A reply that sets one wrong beside another instead of answering the first.
The counter-point is often from a different time or subject, such as an old argument or an unrelated mistake.
It often arrives as a question, which makes it hard to answer without being pulled off course.
It differs from a related issue raised later, because here the new point takes the place of a response.
what_it_sounds_like: What about that time you forgot?
And you've never been late once in your life?
Well, what about when you left me waiting at the airport?
You did the exact same thing last year.
Funny that you bring it up, given how you treated my mother.
If we are keeping score, I could list yours too.
what_it_is_not: Pointing out a true double standard and then returning to the original issue to answer it.
Asking to talk about a related concern after the first one has been dealt with, as a separate conversation.
A comparison that helps explain the point, such as 'I was late too last week, so I understand how it happens'.
A reasonable request that both people apply the same rule, made while still engaging with the complaint.
Two people with overlapping grievances who agree to take turns and keep to it.
this_may_be_it_when: The counter-point is raised before your complaint has had any response.
The topic they raise has no clear connection with what you brought up.
Your complaint is never returned to, even after the other matter has been talked through.
Every complaint you raise is met by one from the past, drawn from a ready list.
You end up defending an old event instead of discussing the new one.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They say 'that is fair, and I would also like to talk about something from my side afterwards'.
The point they raise is directly relevant, such as the same rule being applied unevenly.
Your complaint gets an answer first, even a short one.
The two of you have agreed to cover one subject at a time, and they follow that agreement.
The counter-complaint is not a repeat from earlier arguments but something new to them.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who feel a long-standing grievance has gone unheard may bring it up at any chance because it is on their mind.
A person raised in a household where arguments were fought by trading points may know no other way to disagree.
They may hear your complaint as unfair because of something they remember, and mention it to show that, not to dodge.
common_false_positives: A roommate who says 'I will do the dishes tonight, and can we also talk about the bathroom schedule tomorrow?'
A partner who answers your complaint about lateness with 'you are right, and I felt the same when you were late last month', then discusses both.
An employee who notes that a rule applies to everyone and asks whether it will be enforced evenly.
discernment_questions: Was my original point responded to before the other point came up?
Is what they raise connected to what I said, or is it a different subject?
Does the conversation end with either issue settled?
Do I have a similar list of their faults, and am I tempted to use it the same way?
Would we both agree to deal with one at a time, and stick to it?
less_concerning_if: The counter-point is held for afterwards and actually gets its turn.
They respond to your complaint in a sentence before bringing up their own.
Both of you leave with at least one of the two issues settled.
more_concerning_if: Your complaints are consistently answered with a catalog of your past faults.
The older grievance they raise has already been apologized for and settled.
Raising anything has begun to feel like it will cost you an equal and opposite attack.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself holding back complaints because you expect the answer to be a worse one about you.
The same few old events appear in arguments about unrelated subjects.
Issues you raised a year ago are still open, along with theirs.
You start tracking your own past mistakes so you can defend them quickly.
Whataboutism.repair_check: Your complaint gets an actual answer first, and theirs gets a separate time set aside. A mutual 'we both have faults' that closes the topic leaves your first point exactly as unanswered as before, and may be followed by the same swap next time.
Whataboutism.boundary_respect_check: Try asking for one subject at a time and see what follows. Do they answer the first point, then hold their own for later? Or does the same counter-point come back, louder, as if the order of the conversation were not up for discussion?
Whataboutism.psychological_mechanism: A counter-complaint appeals to a fairness instinct: if you have made mistakes too, pressing your own point can feel unfair. That discomfort can pull attention away from the first complaint, and it tends to work best when the counter-point is true.
Whataboutism.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe feeling that raising anything is pointless because it will be matched with something else. Small issues pile up unspoken. Some begin to feel they owe a running debt of past wrongs, and keep a quick defense of old events ready.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the new point and keep the order: 'That sounds like it matters. Can we deal with the dishes first, and then set time for the birthday?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you will not trade grievances: 'I am willing to talk about your concern. I am not willing to treat it as the answer to mine.'
response_options.disengagement: If each point gets a new one back, stop and say you will return with a single written issue, so only one thing is on the table.
response_options.support_seeking: Write both lists out and show them to a neutral person. They can often tell whether each concern is fair and whether they were ever answered.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a meeting, ask for an agenda with one item at a time and note whose item is being discussed, so that a counter-point is placed on the list and not used to replace the first.

Whataboutism.boundary_script: "You may be right about what happened at the airport, and I want to talk about it. I would like an answer on the money first, and then we can give your issue the same time."
Whataboutism.safety_note: Whataboutism on its own carries no physical danger. It would change if the counter-accusations turn into threats to expose old mistakes, to report you somewhere, or to punish you for raising anything. In that case, write down what is said and speak to someone you trust, or to an advocate or lawyer.
misuse_warning: Calling every counter-point whataboutism can silence a person who truly has a fair, related grievance. The test is whether your complaint gets answered at all.
In public debates the word is sometimes used to wave away a relevant comparison. A fair comparison deserves a real reply.
Whataboutism.how_to_distinguish_from_related: DARVO denies the act, attacks you and casts the speaker as the victim. Whataboutism simply sets a different wrong beside yours. Blame-Shifting says your behavior caused the act at issue, while whataboutism leaves that act alone and talks about another. Denial claims nothing happened, which whataboutism does not.

Non-Apology Apology.short_definition: A statement that sounds like an apology but regrets your reaction or feelings, not the thing that was actually done.
Non-Apology Apology.core_meaning: A statement that sounds like an apology but regrets your reaction or feelings, not the thing that was actually done.
Non-Apology Apology.expanded_definition: A non-apology apology uses the word 'sorry' but does not own the action. The regret is aimed at your feelings, your reaction, or the situation, so the speaker never has to say 'I did that.' Common forms use an 'if', a 'but', or a 'you feel' to move the weight across. Some people were never taught how to apologize and sincerely think this counts. What matters is whether the action is named. A weak apology that does name it is still different from one that never does.
Non-Apology Apology.plain_language_summary: Someone says sorry, but the sorry is about how you took it, not what they did. You are left feeling that nothing was admitted.
Non-Apology Apology.why_this_matters: An apology is how people close a wound and rebuild trust. When the form is there and the substance is not, the hurt stays open and you may feel unreasonable for still being upset after being told sorry.
what_it_is: A statement of regret that points at your reaction or feelings, not at the act itself.
It often contains a hinge word: 'if' you were hurt, 'but' you started it, 'that you feel' this way.
It can be fluent and warm in tone, which makes it hard to explain why it feels empty.
It ends the conversation in the speaker's favor, because after 'sorry' you are expected to move on.
what_it_sounds_like: I'm sorry you feel that way.
I'm sorry if you were offended.
I'm sorry, but you started it.
I apologize that you took it the wrong way.
Sorry you're so upset about this.
I'm sorry you chose to be hurt by it.
Mistakes were made, and I'm sorry it came to this.
what_it_is_not: An imperfect apology that clearly names what was done, such as 'I'm sorry I forgot, that was careless of me'.
A speaker who does not yet understand why something hurt and says honestly, 'I'm sorry it hurt, and I want to understand what I did'.
A sincere expression of sympathy for how someone feels, offered where no wrongdoing is involved, such as at a loss.
A clumsy first attempt from someone who has not learned to apologize, followed by a better one once they are shown how.
An apology in a language or culture where regret is expressed through the situation instead of the person.
this_may_be_it_when: The sentence would still make sense if you removed the action from it entirely.
The word 'if' or 'but' sits right after 'sorry'.
Your reaction is described as the thing to be regretted.
You are expected to say it is fine as soon as it has been said.
The same thing happens again soon after, with the same kind of apology.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The speaker names the specific act, even awkwardly, in the same sentence.
They ask what they could do to put it right and then listen.
The first attempt falls short and they accept correction without defensiveness.
The behavior changes afterwards, whatever the wording.
The regret is about something outside their control, such as bad news, and no one is blamed.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people learned these phrases as children and use them without noticing what they leave out.
Fear of being shamed can make a person reach for vague wording that feels safer than naming the act.
Some formal or professional settings, such as customer service scripts or legal advice, push people toward cautious wording.
common_false_positives: A colleague who says 'I'm sorry this has been such a rough week for you' after a delay that was no one's fault.
A shy teenager who mumbles 'sorry about before' and means the specific thing you both know about.
A company statement that is vague because lawyers wrote it, from a person who privately apologizes properly later.
discernment_questions: Does the apology say what was done, in words that name the action?
Is the regret about my feelings or about their behavior?
Does the sentence have an 'if' or a 'but' that changes its meaning?
What changed after the apology, if anything?
If I explain what was missing, do they take it in or defend the original wording?
less_concerning_if: A second, fuller apology follows once you say what was missing.
The wording is clumsy, but the behavior shifts right away.
They can state back to you what they did and why it hurt.
more_concerning_if: You are told you must accept the apology and are pressured when you do not.
The apology is given with a reminder of your past mistakes, as a trade.
The same act, and the same sort of sorry, come around on a regular schedule.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have heard the same apology wording more than once for the same kind of event.
You have stopped asking for apologies because they never include the part you need.
You find yourself saying 'it's okay' without feeling that it is.
Old hurts stay open because nothing was ever acknowledged enough to close them.
Non-Apology Apology.repair_check: Repair would include the action named in plain words, an acknowledgment that it was theirs, and something that changes afterwards, with nothing asked of you in return. An apology that asks you to feel better, mentions what you did, or repeats unchanged soon after does not close anything.
Non-Apology Apology.boundary_respect_check: What do they do when you ask for the action to be named? A second attempt that says what happened suggests it was heard. Being told you are impossible to please turns the request into a fault in you.
Non-Apology Apology.psychological_mechanism: The word 'sorry' carries social weight, and people tend to forgive on hearing it. A sentence with the shape of an apology but not its content can draw on that habit, so declining it feels rude, and attention shifts from what was done to how you respond.
Non-Apology Apology.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe feeling dismissed even after being told sorry, unsure whether they may stay upset, and sometimes accepting the apology just to end the tension. Over time some stop expecting acknowledgment at all, and old hurts stay open because nothing closed them.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the missing piece: 'Thank you for saying sorry. Could you tell me what you are sorry for? I would like to hear the action named.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say plainly that it does not count yet: 'I appreciate the attempt, but that apology is about my feelings. I need one about what happened.'
response_options.disengagement: You do not have to accept an apology you did not receive. You can say 'I hear you' and leave it there until something more real arrives.
response_options.support_seeking: Read the apology aloud to a friend and ask what it admits. Hearing it from outside can confirm what felt missing and reduce self-doubt.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you need a record, ask in writing for a confirmation of what happened and what will change. Vague apologies in a workplace can be followed up with a specific, dated request.

Non-Apology Apology.boundary_script: "Moving forward is what I want too. What I need is to hear what you did and that it was wrong, not that I feel upset. Can you try saying it that way?"
Non-Apology Apology.safety_note: A hollow apology is not itself a safety signal. It would matter more if it sits in a cycle where harm is followed by sorry, then by harm again, or if refusing to accept it brings anger or threats. In that case, speak to a trusted person or a domestic abuse advocate about the larger pattern.
misuse_warning: Marking every imperfect apology as a non-apology can punish people who are trying and failing at a hard skill. Check whether they name the act and change course.
Demanding exact words from someone, then rejecting each attempt, turns the label into a test no one can pass.
Non-Apology Apology.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Blame-Shifting says your behavior caused theirs, while this tactic need not blame you at all: it regrets your feelings. DARVO denies, attacks and reverses roles. Denial refuses any wrongdoing, whereas here something like a concession is offered and then emptied of the one thing it should contain, the act.

Denial.short_definition: Refusing to accept that any wrongdoing took place, whatever the evidence or how the concern is raised.
Denial.core_meaning: Refusing to accept that any wrongdoing took place, whatever the evidence or how the concern is raised.
Denial.expanded_definition: Denial, as a pattern in conflict, is a blanket 'no' to the idea that the speaker did anything wrong. It is wider than correcting one false detail. It covers the whole event, often in absolute language, and it holds even when specifics or proof are offered. Everyone denies something on first hearing a surprising accusation, so a single no means little. What stands out is a refusal that does not soften, because repair cannot start when nothing has been admitted.
Denial.plain_language_summary: Whatever you raise, the answer is that nothing wrong happened. Details and proof do not change that answer, so there is never a way to start putting things right.
Denial.why_this_matters: If nothing is ever admitted, there is nothing to fix and nothing to forgive. The person raising a concern can be left with the hurt, no acknowledgment, and a sense that the problem was them for noticing it.
what_it_is: A refusal that covers the whole situation, not one disputed detail inside it.
It is phrased in absolutes, such as 'nothing' and 'never', which leave no space for a partial admission.
It stays in place when you offer specifics, a witness or a record.
It can be delivered calmly, with a tone of settled certainty, or loudly, with anger.
what_it_sounds_like: I did absolutely nothing wrong.
I have nothing to apologize for.
None of that is true.
I would never do something like that.
There is nothing to talk about.
I don't know what you are talking about, and I never have.
what_it_is_not: Being wrongly accused and saying so, particularly if the person offers evidence of their own and listens to yours.
Correcting one wrong detail, such as the date or the place, while accepting the rest of the account.
Honest memory failure about something minor that was not memorable at the time.
A brief first reaction of shock that opens into a real conversation once the details are laid out.
A person who disagrees that something was wrong, while willing to discuss why they see it that way.
this_may_be_it_when: The no covers the whole account and not just one point.
It remains the same when you show a message, a photo or a witness.
The words 'never' and 'nothing' keep appearing, even about small matters.
No earlier conflict with this person has ended with them saying they were wrong.
You start to wonder if you are the only one who sees it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They deny one thing and accept others, so the account is divided and not rejected whole.
Their position changes after they see new information.
They can name an example of a time they were wrong, in this or another situation.
The accusation really is mistaken and they can show why.
They say 'I do not remember that' and ask to look at it together.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often deny first and reflect later, so a no on day one can become a yes on day three.
Someone raised to believe that admitting a mistake means being a bad person may find any admission frightening.
A person can honestly believe they did nothing wrong because their view of the event is different from yours.
Fear of consequences at work or in court can lead to a lawyer-style blanket denial.
common_false_positives: A person who disputes one specific claim with documents, while agreeing the rest of your account is right.
A teenager who says 'I didn't do it' on reflex and, a day later, tells you what actually happened.
A colleague who says 'I don't recall that meeting' and truly cannot, and asks to see the notes.
discernment_questions: Is the denial about the whole situation, or about a point inside it?
Has anything I showed them changed their answer at all?
Have they ever, in any dispute, said I was right?
Am I sure of the facts, and is there anything checkable that I could be wrong about?
Would a neutral person looking at the same evidence reach the same view as they have?
less_concerning_if: Their answer softens once they have time to think, or once specifics are on the table.
They hold firm on one point but engage with the rest of your concern.
You can find a record of them admitting fault in other matters.
more_concerning_if: They deny things that are well documented, and carry on denying them in front of others.
The denial comes with pressure on you to drop the subject, or punishment for bringing it up.
You have begun to question your own account, even though you have clear evidence.
pattern_over_time_signs: No dispute with this person has ended with an admission, large or small.
You have stopped raising problems because you expect the same answer.
The same issues come back unchanged because nothing was ever acknowledged.
You hold records of events not for any plan but to remind yourself it really happened.
Denial.repair_check: Repair starts with an admission of at least part of what happened, even a small part, followed by a changed action. 'Let's move on' or 'agree to disagree' offered before anything was acknowledged is the denial under a new name, and the subject stays shut.
Denial.boundary_respect_check: Ask them to look at one specific message or record, not to agree with everything. Whether they look, even if they disagree afterwards, is informative. A refusal to look at all tells you the subject is closed to you.
Denial.psychological_mechanism: Admitting a mistake can threaten a person's picture of themselves, and a flat denial protects that picture at no cost in the moment. For the receiver, repeated confident denial with no witness tends to wear on trust in their own account.
Denial.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe frustration at being unable to settle anything, doubt about whether their own account is accurate, and a slow habit of keeping hurts to themselves. Some feel anger, others a flat tiredness, and some keep records only to remind themselves it happened.

response_options.soft_clarification: Narrow it to one checkable point: 'I do not need you to agree with everything. Could we just look at what the message said on Tuesday?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Stop arguing the whole case: 'I know what I saw, and I am not asking for your permission to remember it. I would like us to talk about what happens next.'
response_options.disengagement: When the answer is a total no, stop presenting the case. Keep your own records, and decide what you will do next without needing them to agree.
response_options.support_seeking: Share your evidence and account with someone who knows both of you, or a counselor. A fair outside view can confirm your reading or point out where you may be wrong.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Move to documents: send a dated summary of what happened and ask for a written reply. Use HR, a mediator or an ombudsperson (an independent complaints officer) if the matter is serious and the denial blocks progress.

Denial.boundary_script: "I am not asking you to agree with everything I said. I am asking you to read this one message with me. If you read it and still see it differently, we can at least start from the same page."
Denial.safety_note: Denial alone does not signal physical danger. It becomes more serious when it follows violence, threats or financial harm, since there is then no acknowledgment that could prevent a repeat. In that case, keep dated records in a safe place and speak with an advocate, a legal aid service or someone you trust.
misuse_warning: People are sometimes labeled as being in denial because they disagree with an accusation. A person can truthfully say they did not do something, and the label should not be used to override that.
Using 'you are in denial' as an argument, with no evidence, shuts down the other person's account in the same way the label describes.
Denial.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Minimization admits something happened but says it was small. Blame-Shifting admits the act and moves its cause onto you. DARVO starts with a denial but goes on to an attack and a role reversal. Plain Denial stops at 'no': there is no counterattack, no excuse and no reduction.

Tone Policing.short_definition: Responding to how something was said and not what was said, so the complaint is never actually discussed.
Tone Policing.core_meaning: Responding to how something was said and not what was said, so the complaint is never actually discussed.
Tone Policing.expanded_definition: Tone policing answers the delivery of a message and leaves its content alone. 'Watch your tone' or 'I won't talk to you like this' may come in reply to a raised voice, a sharp word, or simply visible upset. Asking for calm is often fair, and many conversations do go better after a break. The pattern is in what comes after. If the topic is never returned to, or the objection to tone is raised even when you were calm, delivery becomes a way to avoid the substance.
Tone Policing.plain_language_summary: You raise a problem, and the reply is about how you said it. The problem itself never gets an answer, because the way you spoke always seems to be the issue.
Tone Policing.why_this_matters: People raising real concerns are often upset, and upset is hard to say politely. If tone is always the topic, the people with the most reason to be upset are the ones whose points are never heard.
what_it_is: A reply that deals with volume, wording or emotion and sets aside what you were trying to say.
It often comes with a condition, such as 'when you can say it nicely, I will listen'.
It may be said calmly, which makes the other person look reasonable and you look out of control.
It can also be used in meetings and public settings to wave off a complaint without answering it.
what_it_sounds_like: Watch your tone.
I'm not discussing anything while you're like this.
I won't talk to you when you shout.
Lower your voice with me.
When you can speak calmly, then we'll talk.
You would get further if you were nicer about it.
Take the emotion out of it and I'll listen.
what_it_is_not: A real request to pause a heated talk, followed by actually coming back to it later.
Self-protection from yelling, name-calling or threats, where stepping away is reasonable even if the topic is important.
A person who cannot take in information while overwhelmed, who asks for ten minutes and then returns.
Honest feedback that a particular word or insult hurt, offered along with willingness to hear the rest.
A workplace rule on conduct that is applied evenly to everyone, not only to one complaint.
this_may_be_it_when: The conversation stays on your manner for a long time and never reaches your point.
The tone concern is raised even when you were speaking quietly.
Telling them you will wait until they are ready does not lead to a conversation.
Your content is described as valid only if delivered in a form that costs you something.
The same complaint is met with a tone objection every time you raise it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They propose a break and name a time to resume, then show up.
They answer the substance of your point in the same breath as they ask for calm.
The conversation really did include shouting or insults that would trouble most people.
They hold themselves to the same standard of tone.
Once you slow down, your point gets a real reply.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Raised voices can be frightening, especially for someone with a history of conflict at home, and they may need quiet to think.
Some people truly cannot process content when emotions run high and need time to settle.
Different families and cultures have different norms about volume and directness, and the clash may be about style.
common_false_positives: A manager who says 'let's pick this up after lunch' and puts it on the calendar.
A partner who leaves the room when you shout and returns an hour later asking to talk.
A moderator who asks everyone in a heated public meeting to keep their voices down, and then calls on you next.
discernment_questions: If I said the same thing quietly and politely, would it be answered?
Has the conversation been returned to after tone was raised?
Was my delivery really sharp, or is it described that way whenever I am upset?
Do they apply the same expectation to their own tone?
Is there a version of this conversation, perhaps in writing, where the tone question could not come up?
less_concerning_if: A pause is followed by a real conversation on the substance.
They are open about when and how you can speak so they can listen.
Their own tone is held to the same standard.
more_concerning_if: Even calm, written versions of your complaint are not answered.
Your emotion is described as proof that you are unreasonable or unstable.
Others are told that you are 'always angry', so your concern is dismissed before you speak.
pattern_over_time_signs: You edit your messages many times for sound, and still get comments on how they read.
You have started to hold back your upset until it comes out in a way that proves their point.
Complaints you raised months ago were never answered, only moved aside by a discussion of tone.
You hear your own voice getting smaller in groups where you used to speak freely.
Tone Policing.repair_check: After a break if needed, the conversation goes back to the content, with a real answer to what you asked. A conditional 'I will listen once you are nicer', or an apology for the argument while the complaint sits untouched, leaves the actual subject where it was.
Tone Policing.boundary_respect_check: Compare two moments: how they responded when you were loud, and how they responded when you were quiet and clear. If the answer to the point arrives only in the second case, tone may have been the real issue. If a new objection to tone appears, the standard is moving.
Tone Policing.psychological_mechanism: Most people want to be seen as reasonable, so a remark about tone can lead them to focus on controlling delivery instead of pressing the point. Self-monitoring then takes more of their attention, and the concern gets less.
Tone Policing.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe holding back anger until it is hard to express clearly, rewriting messages again and again, and feeling their emotions are used against them. Some stop raising issues. Others escalate in frustration, which then seems to confirm the criticism.

response_options.soft_clarification: Agree to a calmer delivery and ask for the matching step: 'I can talk more quietly. Will you then tell me what you think about the deadline?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate the two issues: 'If my tone was a problem, I will fix it. That does not answer what I asked.'
response_options.disengagement: If a calm version is still met with objections to tone, put your point in writing and stop having it out loud. A written record is harder to dismiss by volume.
response_options.support_seeking: Show someone neutral the written version of your complaint and ask if it is fair in tone. If it is, you have confirmation that tone was not the real obstacle.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Put the complaint in an email in plain words and ask for a written reply by a date. If tone keeps being used to avoid it, bring it to a manager, HR or an ombudsperson (an independent complaints officer) with the thread.

Tone Policing.boundary_script: "I can speak more quietly, and I will. When I do, I still need an answer to what I asked about the schedule change. Can we agree that you will respond to that once we have both settled?"
Tone Policing.safety_note: Tone policing alone is not a physical danger. It matters more when your upset is described as a threat. It also matters if you are punished for crying or raising your voice, or are afraid to show feeling at all. In those cases, speak with a counselor or advocate, and keep records if the setting is a workplace.
misuse_warning: A request to calm down is often fair, particularly when voices are raised or insults are used. Labeling it tone policing can excuse behavior that really was hurtful.
The label can also be used to avoid hearing legitimate feedback on how a message landed, so check whether the substance still gets heard.
Tone Policing.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Minimization attacks the size of the problem, while tone policing attacks the manner in which it was raised. DARVO denies and then casts you as the aggressor, but tone policing stays on style and may deny nothing. Denial refuses the facts, whereas tone policing never reaches them.
